title: Find the average of all elements in an array (sum / length).
shortTitle: Find the average of all elements in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the average is a two-part linear operation: sum every element in one pass, then divide the sum by the number of elements. For money you accumulate into a `BigDecimal` sum and divide with an explicit scale and `RoundingMode` to avoid non-terminating decimal errors. It is O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to know his average monthly spending at National Bank of India. He adds up all twelve monthly spend figures into one running total, then divides that total by twelve. The result is his typical monthly spend, which he uses for budgeting.
s1_definition.oneliner: Add everything into a running sum, then divide by the count, rounding explicitly because it is money.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the average is a two-part linear operation: sum every element in one pass, then divide the sum by the number of elements. For money you accumulate into a `BigDecimal` sum and divide with an explicit scale and `RoundingMode` to avoid non-terminating decimal errors. It is O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants to know his average monthly spending at National Bank of India. He adds up all twelve monthly spend figures into one running total, then divides that total by twelve. The result is his typical monthly spend, which he uses for budgeting.

**One line to remember:** Add everything into a running sum, then divide by the count, rounding explicitly because it is money.

sections.s2_technical:
You keep a `BigDecimal` running sum initialised to `BigDecimal.ZERO`. You loop once over the elements, adding each with `sum = sum.add(current)`. After the loop you divide by the count.

Division is where money needs care. `BigDecimal.divide` without a rounding specification throws an `ArithmeticException` if the result is a non-terminating decimal, for example ten divided by three. So you always call the overload that takes a scale and a `RoundingMode`, for example `sum.divide(new BigDecimal(count), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)` which gives two decimal places rounded half up, the standard for rupees and paise.

You must guard the empty case because dividing by zero is undefined; averaging nothing has no meaning, so throw `IllegalArgumentException`. Time is O(n) for the single summation pass and space is O(1) for the sum accumulator. A senior nuance is choosing the rounding mode deliberately: HALF_UP is the common banking choice for display, while HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) reduces cumulative bias in large aggregations.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers Rajesh a budgeting insight: "Your average monthly spend." The system holds his monthly spend figures and must compute their average. This is exactly how the average algorithm works — sum then divide.

Problem 2 — Spending figures rarely divide evenly, so the average often has many decimal places. Showing a customer a number with ten decimal places looks broken, and an unrounded BigDecimal division would even crash. This is exactly why we divide with an explicit scale of two and HALF_UP rounding.

The code has an `Account` holding monthly spends and a `SpendAnalyzer` class with a `findAverage` method. The demo computes and logs Rajesh's average spend.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: monthly spends `[12000.00, 15500.00, 9800.00]`.

Step 1 — Guard passes; three elements.

Step 2 — `sum` starts at 0. Add `12000.00`: sum is `12000.00`.

Step 3 — Add `15500.00`: sum is `27500.00`.

Step 4 — Add `9800.00`: sum is `37300.00`.

Step 5 — Divide `37300.00` by `3` with scale 2 and HALF_UP: `12433.33` (the true value 12433.333... is rounded to two places).

Step 6 — Return `12433.33`, which the demo logs.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Average monthly spend for Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001) = Rs.12433.33
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the average of an array is a two-step linear operation. First I sum every element in a single pass, and then I divide the sum by the number of elements. The summation is linear time and I keep only one accumulator, so the extra space is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to give Rajesh a budgeting insight showing his average monthly spend. I accumulate his monthly spend figures into a running total and divide by the number of months.

The part I always stress for a financial system is the division. Every amount is a BigDecimal, and BigDecimal division without a rounding instruction throws an ArithmeticException whenever the result does not terminate, such as a total that does not divide evenly by the count. So I always use the divide overload that takes an explicit scale and a rounding mode, specifically two decimal places with HALF_UP rounding, which is the standard for displaying rupees and paise. I also guard the empty case, because the average of no data is undefined and dividing by zero would crash, so I throw an IllegalArgumentException with a clear message instead. For very large aggregations I would consider banker's rounding, HALF_EVEN, to avoid a cumulative upward bias, but for customer-facing display HALF_UP is the expected behaviour.
